utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This morning we will have a hearing under Rule 62 bis. Its purpose is in accordance with the request of the accused Kolundzija to replead him so that the Chamber may determine whether it is satisfied as to the matters set out in 62 bis. I see Sir Ivan on his feet, but before I ask you to address, I'll just raise some concerns that the Chamber has with the joint motion that has been submitted by the Prosecution and the Defence. If you have the joint motion before you, as you should, I would invite you to look at paragraph C, which is headed "Factual Basis." That paragraph is, in the Chamber's view, exceedingly vague and is not sufficiently precise to allow the Chamber to proceed with the hearing under 62 bis. There is a need for more precision and detail as to the factual basis. Rule 62 bis actually speaks of the sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it, and then it allows for some latitude as to how this factual basis is to be determined, either on the basis of independent indicia or on lack of any material disagreement between the parties about the facts of the case. So what has been provided is not sufficient. The Chamber is, of course, anxious to proceed as expeditiously with this matter, and accordingly we will allow the parties some time to address us orally on this issue. If they are ready to do that now, then we can proceed; if not, we will grant an adjournment. The second matter that I'd like to mention is the second sentence, which again, in the Chamber's view, does not identify with sufficient specificity the sections of the indictment to which the plea relates. This, after all, is a change of plea to the indictment, and it seems to the Chamber that the change of plea relates to paragraph 36(d) and (e) of the indictment, which sets out two of the means by which persecution is allegedly committed. So that again is something on which the parties can address us. And then the last sentence, which indicates that the plea is in satisfaction of all the remaining counts of the indictment, this, of course, is as the counts relate to Kolundzija, and of course, those remaining counts would have to be withdrawn by the Prosecutor. When we actually take the plea, the Chamber would accept either a written or an oral assurance from the Prosecutor that those remaining counts will be withdrawn. But the main concern at this time is with the factual basis as agreed because it is not for the Chamber to search the evidence to identify the factual basis. This is an agreement, and the agreement should show sufficiently the factual basis. Sir Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. I think my learned friend and I have heard clearly what the Chamber has said. We will obviously need a little time for us to comply with the request of the Chamber to produce something in a little more detail, more sufficient detail, to satisfy the Chamber. If my learned friends and I can have the rest of the morning to do that, hopefully we will be able to come back at 2.30 with the answer; if we can't, perhaps we can give some indication to the legal office that it is going to take longer and the Court can, without reappearance, make its views known. I wonder if the Chamber would consider giving us some idea of its programme, on the basis that we are able to agree a more detailed factual basis, over which there may be no difficulty, for the process of the case thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Sir Ivan and Mr. Ryneveld, you could let us know what are the real possibilities of your agreeing something to be ready in time for 2.30, because if there is no real possibility, we would just as soon adjourn until Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I doubt very much there would be a great deal of difficulty in terms of my learned friend and I getting together this morning and agreeing on more specific language, as requested by the Court, but there is a further stage, and that is I understand my learned friend needs access to Mr. Kolundzija in order to discuss the aftermath of that with him, with the translator, et cetera, et cetera. But I'll let my friend talk about that. In terms of my anticipation, at least unilaterally speaking - I haven't had a chance to ascertain with my friend whether or not we will be able to hash out more specific language - I think that is doable within the next couple of hours or so, but I don't know how much time my friend needs after that before he's able to come back to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Sir Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I understand that arrangements have helpfully been made to keep my client here, so as soon as we have come to an agreement about the detail, the detailed references in the transcript or whatever, then I can just go and discuss it with my client. So I think it's reasonably possible that -- reasonably likely that we will be ready by 2.30, but if it begins to look as though we're not going to be, then my suggestion is that we let the office know immediately and then the Court can make its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll adjourn until 2.30, but you will advise us within a reasonable time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- if that is not possible. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld and Sir Ivan, the Chamber has received the Statement of the Agreed Facts, and so that allows us to advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just before we do, if I just might indicate, Your Honours, that in the draft that you may have received, there is a typographical error in paragraph 2, and we would anticipate that a filed copy -- the filed copy which we anticipate filing after the proceedings, will change the date of 1 May to conform with the evidence, which is 24 May. That was just a typographical error. So paragraph 2, about 24 May 1992 to 5 August 1992. That's the only correction that my learned friend and I noted after the copy was provided to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is plain, then, from the admitted facts submitted that the accused Kolundzija will plead guilty to count 3 of the amended indictment, persecution, as set forth in paragraph 36(e) and as described in the document that you have submitted. Paragraph 7 of the document also points out that the Prosecution will withdraw the remaining counts, 4, 5, 6 and 7, upon the Trial Chamber's acceptance of the plea of guilty to count 3. Before I proceed, I think we need to be clear as to how the plea will take place and what precisely is being pleaded to. Sir Ivan, I need to be certain that the accused understands that certain questions will be put to him. In particular, ultimately he will be asked how he pleads to count 3 of the indictment, charging persecution, and in accordance with the agreement, I understand that he will say that he pleads guilty to persecution as set forth in paragraph 36(e) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I have advised --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: So sorry. Yes, Your Honour, and I have advised him that he will be asked certain questions by Your Honour, and he is prepared to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in particular, the last matter that I raised, the plea of guilty in relation to paragraph 36(e), yes. The accused Kolundzija will stand. Stand, Mr. Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have entered into a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor, pursuant to which you will plead guilty to count 3 of the indictment, charging persecution, specifically on the basis of paragraph 36(e) of the indictment, which alleges the confinement of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats and other non-Serbs in inhumane conditions in the Keraterm camp. The Prosecution will withdraw the remaining counts, 4, 5, 6 and 7. Mr. Kolundzija, have you discussed fully with your counsel the plea agreement that you have made with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to enter into the plea agreement? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pursuant to the agreement, the Prosecutor and the Defence have recommended that the Chamber impose a sentence falling within the range of three to five years. You must understand, however, that the sentence will ultimately be determined by the Chamber in accordance with the Statute and the Rules. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kolundzija, how do you plead to count 3 of the indictment, charging persecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am guilty as explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is to say, on the basis of paragraph 36(e), the confinement of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and other non-Serbs in inhumane conditions in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I should say that the Chamber also has in its possession a medical report from Dr. Vera Petrovic, indicating that the accused is completely capable, competent, and sufficiently rational to understand what happens during a trial, to accept changes at individual moments and to decide on them and to understand the consequences of such decisions. The Chamber, having heard all the submissions, is satisfied that the plea has been made voluntarily, that it was informed, that it is not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it. Accordingly, a finding of guilt is entered, and it remains now for us to fix a date for the sentence hearing. I should say in relation to that, before we do that, as I had indicated, the Prosecutor will withdraw the remaining counts in relation to Mr. Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution, in light of the Court's acceptance of the guilty plea to count 3, persecution, now withdraws the remaining counts in this indictment, counts 4, 5, 6, and 7, as against Dragan Kolundzija only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. Mr. Kolundzija, please sit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now have to fix dates for the sentence hearing and for the submission of briefs. The Chamber is naturally disposed to proceeding with this matter as expeditiously as possible. It is a practice of the Tribunal for matters of this kind to be disposed of in a day; at the most, a day and a half or two days. There is really no need for an abundance of witnesses, but naturally it is a matter for counsel to decide. I should also say that counsel should be mindful of the possibility of submitting statements rather than calling witnesses. Bearing that in mind, the Chamber has in mind the dates Tuesday, September the 18th to Thursday the 20th. What we would do is, in consultation now, identify one or two days as is most convenient for all the parties, and the brief would be filed by Friday, the 14th. Mr. Ryneveld first or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I might say that I anticipate that the Prosecution will not be making a lengthy submission, and unless the Court requests, we do not propose to file a written brief with respect to the issue of sentence; simply make a very brief oral representation, unless the Court wants that. The other thing, of course, is a matter of timing with respect to whether or not you wish to deal with this matter separately or whether the Court would like us to deal with the issue at the conclusion of the entire trial with respect to all three accused. We're in your hands in regard to that. I appreciate that my learned friend may wish to prepare a written brief, and we certainly can. I'm simply saying that we do not anticipate taking a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we wouldn't insist on a long brief, but it does seem to us that in a matter of this kind, a brief is important. It need not be very long; just setting out very briefly your recommendations, in particular in relation, of course, to the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It need not be very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you find that to be of assistance, we will certainly have a sentencing brief available by the 14th or whenever you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Sir Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I am concerned about the shortness of time and would ask that the Court, the Chamber, gives me longer. Firstly, we haven't, of course, called any evidence on which we can rely for the purpose of our mitigation, and in particular, we would want to call a medical witness, a psychiatrist, to talk about the effect that all this has had upon the defendant Kolundzija's mental state. My experience of psychiatrists' evidence is it does take a few weeks to get. Furthermore, we would want to call some live witnesses, and they will require some arranging and some selecting in the light of the proceedings that have taken. We also do want to avail ourselves of the opportunity of providing a written brief, and I had rather hoped that, bearing in mind the rest of the case and how it was going to develop apart from Kolundzija, the Court might consider giving us four weeks to achieve that conclusion. It is also rather difficult for me always to get together with my co-counsel, not just because America is a long way away but because they are sleeping when everybody else is awake, and it is -- unless we meet here in The Hague, which also has difficulties sometimes, then it isn't always as easy as if we were both in the same place at the same time. And my experience is that it is much better to allow a reasonable length of time to conclude all these matters finally than it is to put a tight margin on it and find that for some reason, like for example the unavailability of the medical witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many witnesses did you have in mind calling, live witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Obviously nothing like the number we were going to call had the trial proceeded, but several. My learned co-counsel, who has had the dealing with the Defence witnesses, says that he thinks that two days would be an adequate length of time for the calling of evidence, and then, of course, there is speeches, and before then, there will have had to have been the provision of the written brief. In the past, I think the Tribunal has allowed considerable latitude for the Defence in getting their mitigation together, both when the case is yet to be tried and when the case has been being tried, and I would ask the indulgence of the Court to give perhaps a week longer than the Court has indicated it is prepared to give, just so that these matters can be properly finalised, bearing in mind that, for all sorts of reasons, the action of Kolundzija in changing his plea has, I think, been of considerable service to the procedures of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir Ivan. We will consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber has consulted. We take account of the fact that, yes, it has been the practice to allow more time for the preparation of briefs prior to sentence. The next time that would be available to the Chamber is the week beginning Monday the 8th of October. We would then fix the days of Monday the 8th and Tuesday the 9th, with the briefs to be filed by Monday the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are there any other alterations to the schedulings? As Your Honours will recall, I asked you to confirm or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: None so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Might I ask the Chamber, on the 8th and the 9th, we will be calling evidence, and then would you be hearing final speeches, as it were, on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, possibly on the 8th. Depends on how we progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to follow up with what Mr. Greaves said, then in light of -- or with respect of the other two accused in this case, the closing briefs would still be due on the 26th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And closing arguments on the 4th and 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the motion hearing adjourned at
